canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across papers, the prevailing usage is assigning a predefined, discrete, or categorical label to a text input, usually a sentence, sentence pair, document, or entire sequence. Several definitions make the format explicit as taking one text or a pair of texts and outputting a class label based on content, with recurring examples including sentiment, topic, grammatical acceptability, question type, stance, and natural language inference style tasks. A smaller line of work broadens the target from single-label prediction to zero, one, or multiple labels, and success is usually framed as predicting the task label correctly, with some papers mentioning cross-entropy loss or accuracy for the task.

Variants. Papers use the term for a broad family of variants. The most recurrent named variants are topic classification, sentence or sequence classification, and question classification, while other settings include headline and news classification, single-sentence classification, long document classification, and multilingual or cross-lingual, zero-shot, few-shot, and in-context setups. Smaller domain-specific formulations include financial headline, hawkish-dovish, argument unit, deal completeness, and ESG issue identification, plus privacy-policy data practice identification, persuasion strategy classification, note and paper classification, occupation prediction, resume classification, section or sequential sentence classification, problem classification, and text coding; some work also converts visual datasets into text for textual classification.

Space of elicitation and scores. Papers measure text classification with 29 linked instruments, most often AG News, GLUE, TREC, SST-2, and DBPedia. The linked instruments are benchmark datasets and benchmark suites rather than separate scoring rubrics, and they cover topic or news categorization, question classification, sentiment, and broader sequence-classification evaluations. Many other datasets appear in smaller pockets of work.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers link text classification to six constructs rather than to one dominant target. In-context learning is the most recurrent link, with some papers treating it as related to text classification and some measuring it with text classification tasks; other papers use text classification to measure Consistency, Cross-lingual generalization, Prompt sensitivity, and also relate it to Semantic understanding. Overall, papers use it as evidence for several different constructs instead of a single agreed construct.

characterization_sections.label: Space of definitions.
characterization_sections.text: Across papers, the prevailing usage is assigning a predefined, discrete, or categorical label to a text input, usually a sentence, sentence pair, document, or entire sequence. Several definitions make the format explicit as taking one text or a pair of texts and outputting a class label based on content, with recurring examples including sentiment, topic, grammatical acceptability, question type, stance, and natural language inference style tasks. A smaller line of work broadens the target from single-label prediction to zero, one, or multiple labels, and success is usually framed as predicting the task label correctly, with some papers mentioning cross-entropy loss or accuracy for the task.

characterization_sections.label: Variants.
characterization_sections.text: Papers use the term for a broad family of variants. The most recurrent named variants are topic classification, sentence or sequence classification, and question classification, while other settings include headline and news classification, single-sentence classification, long document classification, and multilingual or cross-lingual, zero-shot, few-shot, and in-context setups. Smaller domain-specific formulations include financial headline, hawkish-dovish, argument unit, deal completeness, and ESG issue identification, plus privacy-policy data practice identification, persuasion strategy classification, note and paper classification, occupation prediction, resume classification, section or sequential sentence classification, problem classification, and text coding; some work also converts visual datasets into text for textual classification.

characterization_sections.label: Space of elicitation and scores.
characterization_sections.text: Papers measure text classification with 29 linked instruments, most often AG News, GLUE, TREC, SST-2, and DBPedia. The linked instruments are benchmark datasets and benchmark suites rather than separate scoring rubrics, and they cover topic or news categorization, question classification, sentiment, and broader sequence-classification evaluations. Many other datasets appear in smaller pockets of work.

characterization_sections.label: What it is taken as evidence of.
characterization_sections.text: Papers link text classification to six constructs rather than to one dominant target. In-context learning is the most recurrent link, with some papers treating it as related to text classification and some measuring it with text classification tasks; other papers use text classification to measure Consistency, Cross-lingual generalization, Prompt sensitivity, and also relate it to Semantic understanding. Overall, papers use it as evidence for several different constructs instead of a single agreed construct.
